Data summary of my five flux towers

Author

Merle Braun

Published

November 20, 2026

Introduction

This report provides an overview of five FLUXNET towers and their half-hourly flux and meteorological measurements. The aim is to assess site characteristics, data coverage and the distribution of key environmental variables.

Timestamps are provided in local standard time without daylight-saving adjustments. UTC is used only as a container for storing timestamps in R.

Missing values (-9999) were converted to NA during data import.

C1. Site overview

The five selected flux towers represent different geographical locations and ecosystem types.

C1. Site overview

The five selected FLUXNET towers are located in the United States, Switzerland, Spain, Denmark and Japan.

Geographical distribution

C2. Data coverage

Data coverage was assessed as the proportion of half-hourly NEE observations that were directly measured (NEE_VUT_REF_QC = 0).

The highest data coverage was recorded at DK-Sor (2009), with 80.2% of half-hourly NEE observations directly measured. ## C3. Summary statistics

Summary statistics were calculated for the main flux and meteorological variables at each site.

For precipitation, the mean annual sum was calculated using complete years without missing precipitation values.

C4. Time series

Half-hourly measurements of NEE, GPP and RECO were aggregated to daily means and converted from µmol CO2 m-2 s-1 to g C m-2 d-1 using a conversion factor of 1.0378.

Only days with 48 valid half-hourly values per variable were included in the daily aggregation.

Validation against FLUXMET_DD

The calculated daily NEE values were compared with the official daily FLUXMET product for one site.

Site Days_compared Correlation Mean_absolute_difference
US-Prr 4284 0.9949 0.0489

C5. Diurnal cycles

Mean diurnal cycles of NEE and latent heat flux (LE) were calculated for each site and season.

Meteorological seasons were defined using the latitude of each site. For sites in the Southern Hemisphere, seasons were reversed relative to the Northern Hemisphere.

All five selected sites are located in the Northern Hemisphere.

C6. Interpretation

C6.1. Energy balance closure

Energy balance closure was assessed by comparing the sum of sensible and latent heat fluxes (H + LE) with available energy (NETRAD - G).

Only half-hourly observations with directly measured H and LE values (QC = 0) and available radiation and ground heat flux data were included.

The energy balance was evaluated at site ES-LJu, using 249954 valid half-hourly observations.

The slope of the linear regression was 0.665, with an R-squared of 0.908.

Among the five investigated sites, JP-Hc3 showed the highest annual net carbon uptake. In contrast, ES-LJu showed the lowest net carbon uptake. The largest seasonal variation in NEE was observed at DK-Sor. Differences between the sites may be related to vegetation type, climatic conditions and the length of the growing season. The diurnal cycles revealed differences in carbon uptake and latent heat flux between seasons. I was particularly surprised by high carbon storage of the cropland in Japan. The proportion of gap-filled NEE data varied considerably between the sites, ranging from 32.88 % to 75.86%.
